newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British manufacturing back on track.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British manufacturing back on track.

text.p: Activity in Britain's sluggish manufacturing sector shifted up a gear in September, a leading business survey said on Tuesday, raising hopes that the economy will soon be firing on all cylinders.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said the Purchasing Managers' Index of manufacturing activity rose for the fourth successive month to reach 53.4 percent, its highest level for 17 months, from 52 percent in August.
Output and new orders both recorded the largest monthly increase since Autumn 1994 with the lively domestic consumer sector providing the major source of growing demand.
"Demand has largely stemmed from rising levels of consumers' expenditure which has expanded order books and driven up output levels in firms producing consumer goods," the survey said.
The government pounced on the survey as proof the economic recovery is forging ahead.
"The survey is further evidence that the recovery in manufacturing is strengthening," said Treasury minister Angela Knight.
City analysts said manufacturing, the weak link in the recovery to date, was clearly starting to catch up with the rest of the economy.

"The PMI survey shows the manufacturing sector on the brink of a fully-fledged recovery," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS. "With the worst of the backlog of excess inventories now cleared, the consumer upswing has allowed firms to re-engage in genuine new production."
However, the survey showed that while demand for consumer goods is clearly leading the way, the sickly investment goods sector also saw the first signs of revival.
"In September, growth appears to have filtered down a further level, to producers of investment and goods such as plant machinery," the survey said.

But if companies have started investing in plant and machinery, there was a reluctance to take on more staff. Roughly the same proportion of companies surveyed reported a fall in staff numbers as reported an increase.
And despite the signs of recovery, the survey said there was little evidence greater activity was leading to higher prices.

Commodity prices fell again, although the number of companies reporting a fall in prices dropped to its lowest since January. The prices index rose to 44.0 percent from a revised 41.7 in August, its second consecutive monthly rise.
"Worldwide demand remained weak by historical standards, especially for commodities, driving price competition," the survey said.
This will be of some comfort to Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke who is under growing pressure from the Bank of England to consider a pre-emptive rate rise.

The Bank upped the ante at the July 30 monetary meeting, saying it would prefer to see the cost of borrowing back up at six percent from 5.75 percent currently to give it a better chance of hitting the tough 2.5 percent inflation target.
Underlying inflation has stuck at 2.8 percent for the last four months.
But with a general election looming -- the country must go to the polls by May 1997 -- the chances of Clarke raising the cost of borrowing look slim.
Interest rates are politically sensitive territory in Britain where two-thirds of British households own their own homes and most pay floating interest rates on their mortages.
Clarke will be under intense pressure from his party, currently trailing opposition Labour by over 20 points in the opinion polls, to defer any rate rise until after the election.
